title: Ray Bauduc and Nappy Lamare Interview, 1959-09-09

blocks.x: If you could give your name first, so we'll have it on here just to speak.
Well, I'm Nappy Lamar.
Can you tell just when you were born and where, if you don't mind? Well, I was born in New Orleans. You mean the year? Yes, the year and the date we'd like to have on the birthday.
June the 14th, 1910, in New Orleans, Louisiana.
Did any of your family play music? No, no, nobody. How come you took up music? When did you start?
Well, I used to go around and listen to different bands like Kid Rene and Kid Punch and, oh, quite a few other bands around New Orleans. That's how I got started. I mean, I like music.
Was banjo your first instrument or something else?
No, banjo, well, I played a little trumpet, really. Really? And then I played banjo on a bet.
Oh, really?

Yeah, some kid was playing the trumpet on New Orleans. A kid named Demerrill. And, oh, I don't know, he used to kind of bug me a little, you know? Yeah. The thing about trumpet, I couldn't play trumpet. I said, well, in a month's time I'll play it better than you.
You did at that, huh? Yeah, I was in the band in a month's time. Did you have lessons when you took up the banjo? How old were you, though?
Oh, gee, I don't know, I was a little kid, but, oh, I must have been 13 years old, I guess. 12 years old, at least. And, well, Ray Bauduc's brother taught me how to play banjo. Oh, Ray's brother?

Yeah. Better sit down here, Ray. Well, that's all right, Ray. Just sit down. Sit down. No, no, no, there's plenty of chairs here. I'll just get to do something over here. All right. If you all, maybe we could talk together, and if you wanted one of you to be upstairs, get a little bit of a bed in.
Well, we're glad to do this, man. Yeah.
Yeah, we just said your brother taught him. I was going to ask you, you might give your name, Ray, so we'll have your voice down here recognized.
All right, my name is Ray Bauduc.
Uh-huh. Can you tell when you were born?
Well, I was born and raised down in New Orleans.
You'll have to lean over. I don't pick up anything around here, I think. Huh? What is the birth date?
Well, the birth date? Well, we'll just say just about the same time Jack Benny's tope was born.
He said, that'll be good enough, huh? Yeah, that's good enough. That's okay. Um, was your first instrument drums?
Yes, that's the one and only. I tried the other, but I can't make it. I'll admit what I can't do.
Um, what was your first band when, and who did you start playing?
Well, it was the first band. It was around the house, like Nappy says. My brother used to play banjo. Well, before that he played drums, and...
What was your brother's full name?
Jules, Jules Badoop.
You're still living?
No.
There's one brother of you still living, isn't there?
I got a couple of smaller brothers, younger brothers, yeah.
I know you stopped with them last trip.
And, uh...
Did you have lessons on your drums when you started?

Well, my dad told me I should take lessons, and I went to Kit Peterson down in New Orleans to take lessons, but I couldn't make the grade. I didn't want to play that kind of music. But the son has the music store? No, he used to teach drums around New Orleans. That's, uh, his father. His father? Harold Peterson has a music store. Yeah, I know him. He's out there on Broad Street, not very far from where I used to live there. I'm on one North White Street.
When did you all ever play together for the first time? Not until the Crosby Band? You must have played down there.
No, we used to play out at Spanish Ford, Nappy and I played with Johnny Bison. Come on, get it here, man. That's right, I forgot. I forgot about that.
Sure, he used to play out at Spanish Ford, Tokyo Gardens. My first band was the Owls, New Orleans Owls.
Oh, the Owls, sure. Yeah. Did you make any of the records with them? Yeah, I made... You're on those records, then?
Well, a couple of them. Some of them, yeah. Yeah.
Remember your first record, Ray, that you made, your first group?

Well, the first record I actually made never did come out. It was made in Richmond, Indiana, with Johnny Bisonoff, his band. Oh, yeah. But they never did release those records. It was just a little bit after the Wolverines made their records.
Yeah, one of Johnny's records on OK came out, and Tom Brown and some of them were on that.
Yeah.
But who else?
Well, I made some of those. I don't know which one I made on that. Who was it? I think Monk Hazel made those.
Who were your favorite drummers when you were a kid that you listened to?
Well, Baby Dots and Zootie Singleton. And there was another drummer that came down with... What's that name? Faith Marlowe's band that was on the... Oh, yeah.
You mentioned the other night you couldn't think of the name.

I can't think of his name. He played wonderful drums. No. He did a lot of trick stuff with drums. There were sticks and stuff. Of course, at that time, I was sort of a trick dumber. And a tangle foot dancer and everything else. Yeah. But I finally found out that I got down to the basic part of drums and got the rhythm end of it worked out. That's what I tried to do anyway.
Who were your favorite banjo players, Nappy? Well, really, I... There were none. Did you ever hear of Stale Bread? Yeah, yeah, yeah.
He was a guitar player, but they made homemade instruments, I think, too.
Yeah.

Do you remember him? I never got to know him. I imagine there was some kid on a boat, a colored kid, played a real fine banjo. I don't even remember his name. And he sort of inspired me a little. And also this banjo player with the Rhythm Kings. I don't remember his name. Louis Black. Louis Black. Oh, yeah. In Chicago. Yeah. He played wonderful. Yeah, well, that's...

I listened to him on those records. There's one thing I wanted to ask Ray was telling us the other night, if we don't take all your intermission either, but a little bit about the... a little bit about the two beat, like we were talking about down beat again, and the Crosby period saying that all Dixieland is two beat rhythm. And you were explaining the other night that that's the wrong idea. Oh, well, it isn't the wrong idea.

It's just that everybody has the idea that Dixieland is a two beat rhythm. And that that was brought out. The fact that music came along and progressed a little bit as far as when Benny Goodman came in, he kept a full beat ride. Yeah. And the magazine, like the Metronome and the down beat, they came along and they didn't know how to decipher Dixieland. So they called it two beat and Benny Goodman's style was four beat. Yeah. But as far as Dixieland, the actual beat of Dixieland to me is not two beat. It's on the second and the fourth beat accented. Very lightly. It isn't a oom-ching or nothing like that. Yeah. It's actually accented on the second and the fourth beat of the bar. And, well, I play a sick of patience and I'll play two beats, four beats and mix it up. But all the time I'm doing things like that, I try and keep a little after beat, what we call after beat, accent with my left hand or whatever hand that I'm using for that.
If you're a sock cymbal, do you use that for your...
I use that. I do that quite a bit. I mean, I always try and keep an after beat with the sock cymbal too.
We were talking, I remember Baby Dodds once told me you're the only one that still uses the Chinese crags. Then, well, you told me you have that new...
That's right.
...that new one, the sizzle cymbal.
Well, we got the new sizzle cymbal that we worked out with Mr. Bedeus Zildjian. It came about during the time of the Chinese war, the Chinese war with Japan.
Oh yeah, you couldn't get there.

And we couldn't get any. And I had a crag when I said, well, geez, I got to get something. So I just got together with Mr. Zildjian and had him design a cymbal that sounded something. I can put these rivets in and call it a sizzle cymbal.
Well, I was going to ask Nappy. I keep firing these questions at you so we can get it up. When did you start using this electric bass?

Oh, about, let's see, about two and a half years ago. Is that right, Ray? Yeah, about that. Yeah, last time we went to Chicago. That's right. I picked it up here. I picked up the amplifier here and I just started to play it.
Did you ever use the guitar, the played guitar much?
Oh yeah, on record dates. In fact, we had a record date last week and I used the guitar. Still use the regular six string guitar.
Oh yeah.
I like the guitar.

But some people tune them like four string banjo or something too. Yeah. I think Eddie Conlon knew. No, I tune them on a regular Spanish guitar sound. In the old days in New Orleans, did they use mostly banjo or guitar when you were a kid? First, can you remember that?

Well, they used banjo. They used guitar. Of course they used guitar quite a lot too, you know. The guitar was just starting to come in really. And when I left New Orleans, I went up north and everybody was playing guitar. That was it.
When you left, who did you play with first when you left the city? Did you come north and join a band up here?

Yeah, I went to Chicago first and joined Billy Lussick's band. Tommy Dossier was in the band and Shimmer and Greg, of course Ray was in the band too. And I went back to New Orleans and I came back to Chicago for a month or so and then I went to New York. And then, well, I played around and then I joined Ben Pollock's band.
Can I ask Ray a little bit about when you played with Ben Pollock? Did he just use a stick to the director or what did he do?

Well, he used a stick on a drum, which we got in plenty of arguments about. Well, it was a funny thing. Benny Pollock had the most wonderful band I ever heard in my life. That was including Benny Goodman in the band. They had Jack Teague on and Jimmy McPartland and Big Braider's on piano. I think Dick Morgan was playing banjo and guitar there and Harry Goodman on bass. I think Al Harris played first trumpet. And the saxophone, well, of course, they had Gil Roden and Benny Goodman and Larry Binion, I think, was the first saxophone player when I joined the band. And then later on I had, oh, I can't figure this, saxophone. Anyway, the tenor man. But that was a wonderful band and that band was built around Benny Pollock. Benny had a funny beat. He used the brushes quite a bit. And when I joined the band, I had to learn how to play like Benny Pollock and make the band swing. I couldn't swing the band. It was funny, but that's the truth. And I tried to play as close to what he did to make the band sound good as I could. Well, of course, later on he used to sit in the band and he'd play especially here and there. He'd teach it himself. That's right. Well, naturally, because he was out in the front. But when the band wouldn't get swing right, the drums were right down in the front of the band, right in the middle. And he'd start beating on cymbals and I'd just stop playing. I said, well, you take it, man. Here's the stakes. We'd argue about it because, after all, if he wanted me to play, and I was a little guy, a little wiry-eyed guy, you know. So I wanted to do things too, but he wanted the band to swing his way. Well, naturally, the band swung that way and that's the way he wanted to do it. So I tried to do the best I could to copy everything that he did to make the band go that way. But later on, he finally got away from the assembly, found out that I was doing all right, and naturally I elaborated on different things that he did and went on into my own style.
Well, are you watching the time? Yeah. How much? We don't want to take off your whole intermission.
It's not like five minutes here.

Yeah, well, I guess you all want to get upstairs and get a little recreation too. We certainly appreciate your interview. Is there anything else you'd like to add, just briefly, about your life or the period with Crosby? I think that's been pretty well written up, of course. Everybody knows the Bobcats.
Well, that was a wonderful band too.
Yes, I know that.
I mean, that band, that was originally the Pollock band that migrated on into the Crosby band. And a few people like Crosby band.
I guess you enjoyed working with Crosby band.
Well, I never had a better bunch of musicians to work with in my life. I thought it was the greatest band I ever played in the Crosby band.
How long have you all been in California now? Oh, I moved out there in 43. You've been about that long too, Ray?

Yeah, well, in 42 is when the Crosby band broke up and I went to service for about three and a half years. And then when I came out again, I got a home there myself, see? Yeah. So we have our homes out there in California now. Yeah. But I still like New Orleans.

Well, I hope so. Me too. When you get back home to New Orleans, we'll have more time in the home. Maybe a half hour interview or so for each one of you. I hope so. And because they're putting us in the Tulane Library, you might say. Oh, that's wonderful. So your voices will be preserved and the information about all the news stations that come from there. Oh, that's nice. I hope to interview you last fall there when you were on the riverboat that night, remember?
Oh, yeah. Well, yeah, I think it was October the 13th when we played with Doc Shue showing and the whole gang down there. Oh, that was a wonderful deal. All our families.
Wow.
But I knew there was such a big reunion then. We didn't have time for you. And I was in California last year and I knew you were busy working there at 400 Club, so...
I didn't have much time down there, but I did have some good crawfish and some voices and stuff that they got down there.
We mustn't take any more of your time from this intermission.
Well, wonderful.
Thank you very much. Thank you very much for your kind attention and time. Thank you. Good stuff very much. Thank you.
